subject: Business
title: Bretton Woods: The Dollar Rules the World
description: Learn Bretton Woods: The Dollar Rules the World in one minute.

hook.text: In 1944, 44 nations gathered in New Hampshire and agreed: the US dollar would anchor the global economy.

buildup.text: Bretton Woods pegged all currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 per ounce.

discovery.text: This gave the world stable exchange rates and the US an enormous privilege: its currency was everyone's reserve.

twist.text: By the 1960s, the US printed more dollars than its gold could back. France demanded gold; the system cracked.

climax.text: In 1971, Nixon ended gold convertibility. The dollar was now backed by nothing but trust in the US government.

punchline.text: Since 1971, all money is backed by trust. Nothing else.

quiz.question: What happened in 1971 that changed global money?
options: Nixon ended the dollar's convertibility to gold
The US returned to the gold standard

details.summary: The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement established the US dollar as the world's reserve currency, pegged to gold at 35 dollars per ounce, with other currencies pegged to the dollar. This system created the IMF and World Bank and shaped the postwar global financial order.
details.whyItMatters: Bretton Woods established American financial dominance that persists today. Understanding this system explains why the US dollar remains the global reserve currency and why its monetary policy affects every nation on earth.
takeaways: The 1944 agreement pegged the dollar to gold and other currencies to the dollar
The IMF and World Bank were created to manage international finance
Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971, transitioning to floating exchange rates

faq.question: Why did the Bretton Woods system collapse?
faq.answer: US spending on Vietnam and domestic programs created more dollars than gold reserves could back. Foreign governments began demanding gold for their dollars. In 1971, Nixon suspended gold convertibility to stop the drain, effectively ending the system.

faq.question: Why is the US dollar still the world's reserve currency?
faq.answer: Inertia, deep liquid financial markets, US military power, and the fact that global oil is priced in dollars all sustain its dominance. About 60 percent of global foreign exchange reserves are still held in dollars, though this share has gradually declined.
